chapters.title: Chapter 3: Risk, Returns and the Power Law

lessons.title: The Power Law: Why One Winner Pays for the Whole Portfolio

children.text: In July 2010, according to a YourStory account, an angel investor put ₹10 lakh into a young Delhi company called Zomato. At the IPO price of ₹76 per share in July 2021, that stake was reportedly worth about ₹150 crore, roughly 1,500 times the original cheque. Think about what that means: one such investment could absorb the total loss of 1,499 other ₹10 lakh cheques and still break even. In the last lesson, you saw how often startups fail. This lesson explains the other half of the story, the power law, and the portfolio rules it forces on every serious angel.

body.text: In angel investing, returns are not spread evenly. A tiny fraction of investments produces most of the gains. Your job is not to avoid every loser; it is to make sure you own the rare, enormous winner when it arrives, and to still own it when it matters.

children.text: Two Kinds of Worlds

markDefs.definition: A pattern where a very small number of outcomes are vastly larger than all the rest combined, so averages are dominated by a few extreme cases.
A single result far outside the usual range, such as one startup returning 100x while most return nothing.

children.text: Most things you measure in daily life cluster around an average: heights of adults, marks in a class, the time your commute takes. Startup outcomes follow a
power law
instead. There is no meaningful "typical" result, because one
outlier
can outweigh everything else put together.

columns.label: Average-driven world
points: Examples: heights, exam marks, a bank FD's interest
Most results sit close to the average
No single result changes the total much
Sensible strategy: avoid mistakes, aim for the middle

columns.label: Outlier-driven world
points: Examples: startup exits, book sales, city populations
Most results are small or zero
One result can be larger than all others combined
Sensible strategy: make sure you own the outliers

children.text: What the Data Shows

Two widely cited datasets from the US venture industry show the same shape. Horsley Bridge, an investor in venture funds, shared data on about 7,000 investments made between 1985 and 2014. Correlation Ventures studied about 21,000 venture financings. Indian data this detailed is not publicly available, but the Indian examples in this course follow the same pattern.

children.text: Farah vs Kabir: Why the Size of the Winner Is Everything

In the last lesson, Farah put ₹5 lakh into each of 20 startups and ended with 1.375x, worse than an FD, despite one 20x winner. Now meet Kabir. His portfolio is identical in every way except one: his best company returns 100x instead of 20x.

body.caption: Same portfolio, different winner (₹5 lakh in each of 20 startups, illustrative)

body.title: Where Kabir's ₹537.5 lakh came from (₹ lakh)
How much came from one company?
body.prompt: Kabir's portfolio returned ₹537.5 lakh in total, of which ₹500 lakh came from his single winner. What percentage of his total returns came from that one company? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: ₹500 lakh ÷ ₹537.5 lakh = 0.930, or about 93%. The other 19 companies together contributed about 7%. Change one outcome and the entire portfolio goes from worse than an FD to far better than the Nifty's long-run average.

children.text: You can flip the question around and ask how big a winner you need to reach a target. With equal cheques across N startups:

body.latex: \text{Winner multiple needed} = (\text{Target portfolio multiple} \times N) - \text{Sum of all other companies' multiples}
body.caption: For Farah's portfolio, the other 19 companies add up to 5 × 0.3 + 3 × 2 = 7.5x. To make 2x overall: 2 × 20 − 7.5 = 32.5x from the winner.

body.title: What does 3x require?
body.prompt: Using the same 20-startup portfolio, where the other 19 companies add up to 7.5x, what multiple must the single winner return for the whole portfolio to reach 3x?
body.explanation: 3 × 20 = 60. 60 − 7.5 = 52.5x. A 3x portfolio, a good but not spectacular result for angel investing, needs one company to return more than 50 times its cheque.

body.text: Put a 100x return into rupees. If your ₹10 lakh entered at a ₹10 crore post-money valuation and later rounds dilute you to 0.4%, returning ₹10 crore needs the company to exit at ₹10 crore ÷ 0.4% = ₹2,500 crore. At seed, you are not asking "is this a good business?" You are asking "could this realistically become a ₹2,500 crore company?"

children.text: Look at 2012. Selling at 5x, or 11x, would have been a great result by any normal standard, and it would have cut this angel's eventual outcome by more than 99%. The power law punishes selling winners early at least as harshly as it punishes backing losers.
Four Rules the Power Law Forces on You
Own enough companies to catch a winner.
If you back three startups, you are betting your whole result on finding a rare outlier in a tiny sample.
Judge deals by upside, not safety.
A company that can only ever become a nice ₹50 crore business cannot pay for your losses, however safe it looks.
Do not sell your best companies too early.
If you need liquidity, consider selling part of a winning stake and keeping the rest.
Keep reserves for follow-ons in the companies pulling ahead.
Many angels hold back part of their budget to use pro-rata rights in their strongest companies, not to rescue weak ones.

Rule 1 is pure probability. Suppose each startup you back has a 3% chance of becoming a big winner, and outcomes are independent. The chance you own at least one winner rises with the number of companies:

body.caption: p is the chance any single startup becomes a big winner (3% here, an illustrative assumption), and N is the number of startups you back.

body.title: Chance of owning at least one big winner, at 3% per startup (illustrative)

body.text: The power law is not permission to back anything. Owning 50 weak deals gives you 50 chances at nothing, because a big winner only helps if it is actually in your portfolio. Access to good deals and sound selection still matter. Also beware survivorship bias: stories like the Zomato angel are told precisely because they are rare, and for every one of them there are many angels whose portfolios never found an outlier.

body.title: The costliest mistake
body.question: According to power-law thinking, which of these mistakes usually costs an angel portfolio the most?
options: Losing ₹5 lakh on a startup that shuts down
Selling the portfolio's best company at 5x when it could have become 200x
Paying a platform fee of ₹10,000 on a deal
Backing a startup that returns exactly 1x
body.explanation: A shutdown can cost at most the cheque. Exiting a future 200x winner at 5x gives up 195x on that cheque, which is often more than the value of every other company in the portfolio combined. Fees and 1x outcomes are minor by comparison.

body.title: Neel's secondary offer
body.scenario: Neel, a Hyderabad angel, has invested ₹5 lakh in each of 12 startups, ₹60 lakh in total. Six have shut down and five are uncertain. One fintech has done extremely well, and a later-stage fund now offers to buy Neel's entire stake for ₹1 crore in cash, 20x his cost. The company is still growing fast and plans a large round next year.
body.prompt: Should Neel sell the whole stake? Think it through using the power law.
body.modelAnswer:
1. This company is almost certainly Neel's portfolio. Six shutdowns and five uncertain companies mean the fintech is carrying his entire result, so this decision matters more than all his other decisions combined.
2. ₹1 crore on ₹60 lakh invested already makes his whole portfolio profitable at about 1.67x from this stake alone, which is a genuine achievement worth locking in partly.
3. Selling everything caps his upside at 20x. If the company keeps growing, the stake could be worth several times more, and the power law says that is where the big returns come from.
4. A balanced option is a partial sale: for example, selling enough to recover his full ₹60 lakh and keeping the rest as a free-carried position in the winner.
5. He should also weigh his personal finances, how concentrated his net worth has become, the company's actual growth and cash position, any restrictions in the shareholders' agreement on selling, and the tax on the gain. The worst reason to sell everything is simply the relief of seeing a big number.

body.title: Remember the data
body.textWithBlank: In Horsley Bridge's data on about 7,000 venture investments, roughly 6% of deals produced about ___% of total returns.
body.explanation: About 6% of deals, each returning 10x or more, generated roughly 60% of all returns. A small number of outliers dominates the result.

cards.definition: A pattern where a few outcomes are vastly larger than all others combined, as with startup returns.
A single result far outside the usual range, such as one startup returning 100x.
Drawing conclusions from the famous successes you hear about while ignoring the many failures you do not.
Backing many startups without real selection; diversification without quality rarely finds a winner.
Putting more money into an existing portfolio company in a later round, ideally one that is pulling ahead.
Selling part of a winning stake to another investor to lock in gains while keeping some upside.

points: Startup returns follow a power law: in Horsley Bridge's data, about 6% of deals produced about 60% of returns, while about 65% of financings in Correlation Ventures' data returned less than 1x.
The size of your best winner matters more than your hit rate: the same portfolio returns about 1.4x with a 20x winner and about 5.4x with a 100x winner.
Winner multiple needed = target portfolio multiple × N − sum of the other companies' multiples; a 3x portfolio of 20 can need a 50x-plus winner.
At seed, ask whether a company could realistically reach a very large exit value, not just whether it is a decent business.
Diversify enough to catch a winner, but only across deals you have genuinely selected; quantity without quality does not work.
Selling your best company too early can cost more than all your failures combined; consider partial sales instead.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The Zomato angel figures are as reported by YourStory and have not been independently verified. Venture return data comes from US datasets and may not reflect Indian outcomes. Farah, Kabir, Neel and all portfolio figures are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
